name: Prize crossword No 21,909
preamble: One word (either in its singular or its plural form) is commonly associated with each of the across solutions, but is not defined in the clues

clue.text: It's tricky when hot

blocks.note: surface reading: something that is hard to handle while it is still hot
setter's reading: a vegetable which, prefixed by the word hot, becomes an idiom for an awkward issue nobody wants to hold

explanation.surface: A warning about some dish or object that becomes awkward to handle once heated.
explanation.walkthrough: A hot potato is an idiom for a controversial problem. The theme word, never clued, is SWEET: every across answer can follow it, as in sweet potato.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a contentious matter people pass along quickly, just as they would drop a scalding vegetable.

clue.text: Naughty dog, maybe, swal-lowed cricket club article

indicators.note: whatever is swallowed ends up inside the swallower

blocks.note: a dog is one example of a pet
CC is the abbreviation for cricket club
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A badly behaved dog that gobbled up something belonging to the cricket club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naughty dog' wants to be read together, but the definition stops at the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Peccant is a formal word for sinning or offending, so it describes someone guilty of misbehaviour.

clue.text: Red's first in every French rainbow?

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
placing something in another word puts it inside

blocks.note: the French word for every or all
the opening letter of the colour

explanation.surface: Asking whether red always comes first in a rainbow, French-style.
explanation.walkthrough: The rainbow looks like the spectrum of colours, but it is a freshwater fish; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The rainbow is a species of this fish, so the word is defined by naming one kind.

clue.text: Adjust short lens? There's no point!

definitions.note: a phrase standing for an adjective

indicators.note: to adjust is to alter or rearrange, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A photographer told to adjust a stubby lens complains it is pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There's no point' sounds like exasperation, but it is literal: a stem with no sharp spines.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants with this quality lack prickles, so no sharp spike is present anywhere on the stem.

clue.text: Shall I finish with half a dram?

indicators.note: taking only half of a short word means discarding its other two letters

blocks.note: 'will I?' is another way to ask 'shall I?'
the back half of this four-letter word for a nip of whisky

explanation.surface: A drinker wondering whether to end the evening on half a measure of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Across clues carry wordplay only; the unclued theme word SWEET goes in front, making sweet William, a garden flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet William is a cottage-garden flower with clustered blooms; the theme word supplies the missing half of the phrase.

clue.text: Girl's bathing in re-bottled wine ... in what?

indicators.note: bottling something again moves it around, so these letters are rearranged
someone bathing sits immersed inside the liquid

blocks.note: taken as written
'girl's' as a possessive is her

explanation.surface: A girl lounging in a bath of wine, and someone asks what she is in.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins a scene to a question; the closing question is the definition, a formal word for 'in which'.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic interrogative adverb asks in which place or respect, the formal equivalent of the question.

clue.text: Authorised lecturer, here for "Proust on Time"

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for lecturer
the French word for here, as the French novelist would say it
T is the abbreviation for time, placed after

explanation.surface: An approved academic arriving to give a talk about Proust and time.
explanation.walkthrough: Proust's great novel is about time, so the quoted title looks like a lecture topic; really he just signals French.
explanation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful or permitted, so something sanctioned by authority is legitimate in this sense.

clue.text: Built into a clue to give one the needle?

indicators.note: building assembles components to form a new structure

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter planting something in a clue just to irritate the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give one the needle' is British slang for annoy, but here it is literal: a jab with a syringe.
explanation.definitionFit: Inoculating a patient means injecting a vaccine, typically by syringe, hence a needle.

clue.text: Profane Calliope, for one, is taken in

indicators.note: something taken in is held inside

blocks.note: Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry
taken as written

explanation.surface: A goddess of poetry described as irreverent and deceived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Profane' looks like an adjective, but it is the verb meaning to treat something sacred with disrespect.
explanation.definitionFit: To profane is to abuse or desecrate something holy, so it means treating it wrongly or abusing it.

clue.text: A desperate chap takes up little time for capers

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Desperate Dan is the strongman of the British comic The Dandy
a sec is a short moment

explanation.surface: A man at the end of his tether spends a short while pulling stunts.
explanation.walkthrough: Desperate Dan, the cow-pie-eating cowboy of The Dandy comic, gives DAN; 'desperate' is part of his name, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Capers are playful skipping leaps, so lively movements to music count as the same thing.

clue.text: EC protocols had to be redrafted

indicators.note: a redrafted text has its wording rewritten into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written: all fourteen letters

explanation.surface: European Community regulations had to be written again.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no definition: the theme word SWEET goes in front of every across answer, and chocolate drops are sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Small disc-shaped confections of cocoa are sold as children's treats, fitting the unclued theme word perfectly.

clue.text: Gas enveloped this Roman

indicators.note: to envelop is to wrap around, so one piece goes outside another

blocks.note: CS gas is the tear gas used in riot control
the Latin word for 'this'

explanation.surface: A Roman figure engulfed in gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' signals Latin, the language of ancient Rome. The unclued theme word SWEET fits: sweet chocs.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocs is informal British shorthand for chocolates, the boxed confections associated with the theme word.

clue.text: Notes negative feedback

indicators.note: feedback sends a signal back the way it came, so letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: two musical notes, A and F
the word of negation

explanation.surface: Someone writes down unfavourable comments from an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: With the theme word SWEET in front, this is Robert Burns's song 'Flow gently, sweet Afton', about a Scottish river.
explanation.definitionFit: Afton Water is an Ayrshire river immortalised in a Burns poem, whose famous line attaches the theme word.

clue.text: Bust heads?

blocks.note: the bust is the upper front of the torso
nut is slang for head

explanation.surface: A sculptor's busts, or someone breaking heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a verb meaning break, but it is the torso. The theme word SWEET goes in front: sweet chestnuts are the edible kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet chestnut tree yields edible nuts roasted in winter, unlike the inedible horse variety.

clue.text: Swell to look over?

indicators.note: turning something over flips it so it reads the other way round

blocks.note: a swell and a toff are both old slang for a smartly dressed upper-class man
to look is to see

explanation.surface: A posh gentleman being invited to inspect something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' is a noun here, not a verb; a toff is British slang for a posh person. The theme word SWEET fits: toffees are sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Chewy confections of boiled sugar and butter are classic sweets, matching the unclued theme word.

clue.text: It brightens up bad French party turning into a fiasco

indicators.note: turning round makes letters run backwards
going into something puts it inside

blocks.note: the French word for bad
a do is a party
a fiasco is a flop

explanation.surface: Something cheers up a dreadful French party that becomes a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' looks like an anagram signal, but with 'French' it gives the French word; the whole pair turns round and sits inside the failure.
explanation.definitionFit: A powerful lamp throwing a broad beam lights up a stadium or building, illuminating the scene.

clue.text: Treatment for a bitten off tongue

indicators.note: something bitten off loses its tip, so a final letter is cut
a treatment works material over, so these letters are processed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Seeking first aid for someone who has bitten through their tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a medical query; in fact the tongue is clipped and mixed with A. The unclued theme word SWEET fits: nougat is a sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A chewy confection of honey, sugar and nuts is sold as a sweet, matching the theme word.

clue.text: Pole vaulters aim for the door

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective describing that type of door

blocks.note: first meaning: what a vaulter hopes to do at the bar
second meaning: a garage door that swings upward and back into the roof

explanation.surface: Athletes clearing a bar head for the exit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole vaulters' looks like Polish athletes or a description of people; it is simply the event. The second meaning is a style of garage door common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaulter must rise and clear the bar, and that same hinged motion names a common garage door design.

clue.text: Sometimes a mickey-taking society ...

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside

blocks.note: Mickey is a famous cartoon rodent, so this animal is sometimes a Mickey
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A group devoted to teasing, left trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mickey-taking' looks like the British idiom for teasing, but it splits into Mickey Mouse and taking. The theme word SWEET fits: a sweet mousse is a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A light whipped dessert, often chocolate, is a sweet course, which the unclued theme word supplies.

clue.text: Measures taken by printers seen working around old hack

indicators.note: something working is in motion, so these letters move about
going around something encloses it

blocks.note: taken as written
a nag or hack is a worn-out horse

explanation.surface: Printers at work being observed around a weary journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hack' suggests a veteran reporter beside printers, but it is the horse. An ennage is a printer's count of ens, a unit of type width.
explanation.definitionFit: Typesetters reckon text length in ens, so counts of these units are measurements used in the print trade.

clue.text: ... filled old education department with fury

indicators.note: something filled has material packed inside it

blocks.note: the former UK Department of Education and Science
fury is rage

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the teasing society enraged an old government department.
explanation.walkthrough: The DES was the British government's education ministry until 1992. The theme word SWEET fits: dragees are sugar-coated sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar-coated almonds or silver cake balls are confections, the kind of item the unclued theme word suggests.

clue.text: Older members accomplish their desires

blocks.note: to do is to accomplish
yens are longings or yearnings

explanation.surface: Senior club members finally get what they want.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence, but splits into a definition and a two-word charade.
explanation.definitionFit: A doyen is the most senior or respected person in a group, so these are its veteran figures.

clue.text: They tend to involve one in unnatural stress

indicators.note: unnatural means not in the normal state, so these letters are out of order

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A general observation that some people tend to drag others into strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tend to' looks like 'are inclined to', but 'They tend' is the definition: in Britain a sister is a senior nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior nurses in British hospitals carry this title and look after patients on the ward.

clue.text: Count the receipts from first class? A pushover!

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
pushed over, letters are knocked out of their order

blocks.note: opening letter of class
the article and the first four letters of the last word, which splits into push and over

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper finds counting the first-class takings easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First class' looks like a single phrase and 'pushover' a single word; both split.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashing up is totting the day's takings in a till at closing time in a shop.

clue.text: Plus fours: five of them

blocks.note: plus means and
five fours make twenty

explanation.surface: Counting a set of golfing trousers, plus fours, five pairs of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Plus fours are baggy knee-length golfing trousers; here the phrase splits into plus and fours. With SWEET it is Feste's 'Then come kiss me, sweet and twenty' from Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespearean song phrase addresses a young sweetheart, so the theme word completes a familiar literary quotation.

clue.text: A go-between for smokers taking Ecstasy

blocks.note: taking and with both mean accompanied by
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A drug dealer serving smokers who also take ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The smokers are chimney flues, not people; a withe is the brick partition separating flues in a chimney stack.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin wall dividing adjacent flues sits between the smoking chimneys, separating them like an intermediary.

clue.text: See 9
Work (some hope!) rapidly

indicators.note: some means a portion, so only part of the text is taken

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone hoping a job gets done fast.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket hides the indicator in an aside. Opus means work in Latin, and its plural is the answer, which also names a musical drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera is the plural of opus, a creative composition, so it denotes works.

clue.text: Cardinal cunning?

blocks.note: His Eminence, the title of a cardinal
art can mean craft or guile

explanation.surface: A churchman's crafty scheming.
explanation.walkthrough: HE stands for His Eminence, the formal style of a cardinal. With the theme word SWEET it makes sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is a beloved partner, a phrase formed by the theme word plus this organ.

clue.text: Hackman and First Lady hugged Violet

indicators.note: a hug wraps arms around someone, so outer pieces enclose an inner one

blocks.note: Gene Hackman, the American actor
Vi is the short form of the name Violet
Eve was the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: An actor and a president's wife embracing a woman named Violet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife but means Eve; the two names together surround Vi. With SWEET it is the old song 'Sweet Genevieve'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian ballad title and the 1953 veteran-car film both pair this name with the unclued theme word.

clue.text: Pages engaged by the Lords

indicators.note: to be engaged is to be taken on or held, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: members of the House of Lords are peers
pp is the abbreviation for pages

explanation.surface: Young pages employed in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Pages look like servants, but they are the abbreviation pp. The theme word SWEET fits: sweet peppers are the mild bell kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Mild bell capsicums are sold as sweet peppers, distinguishing them from fiery chilli varieties.

clue.text: Read out document

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so these letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: An instruction to recite a paper aloud to an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read out' looks like one phrasal verb; the first word is the fodder and the second scrambles it. With SWEET it is the goodnight wish 'sweet dreams'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying sweet dreams wishes someone pleasant visions in sleep, a stock bedtime phrase using the theme word.
